items.title: The earliest Christians thought Jesus would return within their lifetime
items.claim: Paul's letters (50s CE) are the oldest Christian texts. What does he tell his churches about the timing of Christ's return?

options.text: He explicitly warns that it will be many centuries away
He tells believers — in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 — that 'we who are alive, who are left' will be caught up to meet the Lord
He refuses to discuss the timing at all
He places the return precisely at AD 70, the destruction of the Temple

items.reveal:
1 Thessalonians 4:15-17, written around 50-51 CE, includes Paul among those still alive at the Parousia. 1 Corinthians 7:29 says 'the appointed time has grown short.' Mark 9:1 has Jesus saying 'some standing here will not taste death' before seeing the Kingdom.

When Christ did not return, later texts (e.g. 2 Peter 3:8 — 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years') reinterpret the delay. This shift is one of the central transformations of early Christian theology.
items.why: Treating the New Testament as a unified, settled doctrine misses that it documents a community reinterpreting itself in real time. The 'delay of the Parousia' is one of the formative pressures on Christian thought.

items.title: Jihad means 'struggle' — and has a greater inner meaning
items.claim: What is the classical Islamic distinction between greater and lesser jihad?

options.text: Greater jihad is large-scale war; lesser jihad is small skirmishes

A widely cited hadith distinguishes the 'lesser jihad' (armed struggle in defence of the community) from the 'greater jihad' (the inner struggle against one's own ego) — though the hadith's authenticity is debated by some scholars
Jihad means only armed warfare; it has no inner meaning
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Scholars including Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and modern critics question the hadith's authenticity. But the inner-struggle understanding is found independently in Sufi traditions and in mainstream piety.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.

items.title: Kosher laws separate meat and dairy in cooking, eating and utensils
items.claim: What are the main kashrut restrictions?

options.text: Permitted animals (mammals chewing cud with cloven hooves; fish with fins and scales); ritual slaughter (shechita) by a trained shochet; separation of meat and dairy; prohibitions including pork, shellfish and mixing milk and meat
Only meals at synagogue must be kosher

items.reveal:
The meat-dairy separation derives from three repetitions of 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk' (Exodus 23:19, 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21). Rabbinic interpretation extended this to all mixing.

Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 list permitted and forbidden animals. Pork and shellfish are the most widely known prohibitions; rabbit, camel and birds of prey are also forbidden.

Shechita is ritual slaughter by a perfectly sharp knife in a single cut, designed to be quick and to drain blood. Some European countries (Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Belgian regions, Denmark) have banned shechita without prior stunning on animal-welfare grounds — a continuing source of dispute.
items.why: Religious practice is often embodied — daily eating, household kitchens, separate dishes. Kashrut is one of the clearest cases of belief expressed through bodily and domestic practice.
